title: Why are mummies frightening?
subtitle: From tomb to screen
subject: mythologie
description: The Egyptians embalmed their dead to protect them, not to scare the living. It took apothecaries, journalists and Hollywood to turn the mummy into a monster.
author: angela-bouma

hero.hook: A corpse is supposed to disappear. The mummy refuses, and that is exactly what unsettles us.

blocks.text: Most bodies decay. A mummy does not. It is visibly dead, yet it still looks human: skin, hair, teeth and facial features can survive for **centuries**. The fear it inspires has little to do with violence. It comes from a body that stubbornly refuses to disappear.

The **Egyptian** mummy is the most familiar, but many climates preserve bodies. Deserts, ice, peat bogs and salt do it naturally. Deliberate [[mummification]] reaches the same result on purpose: the body is dried, the organs removed, the whole covered in resins and wrappings. Either way, a body is held onto long after death should have taken it.

sections.title: Preserving the body for the afterlife

blocks.text: No country is more closely tied to mummies than **Egypt**. The tradition took shape there over thousands of years, alongside beliefs about death and the afterlife. Preserving the body allowed the dead person to go on existing. The body was therefore at the heart of Egyptian funerary rites.

blocks.caption: Anubis, the jackal-headed god, embalms a mummy. Tomb of Sennedjem, Deir el-Medina.

blocks.text: The earliest burials relied on the dry heat of the desert. Little by little, embalmers refined their methods. Under the [[New Kingdom]], roughly **1550 to 1070 BC**, wealthy Egyptians received elaborate treatment: organs removed and preserved separately, the body dried with [[natron]], then rubbed with oils and wrapped in linen.

None of this was meant to create a monster. The mummy stood for **preservation** and religious continuity, within a system built to protect the dead, not to frighten the living. That meaning only shifted once the mummy left the place it was made for.

sections.title: From sacred relic to powdered remedy

blocks.text: The meaning changed as soon as mummies reached **Europe**. In the Middle Ages and then the early modern period, Europeans encountered them through trade, travel and the study of antiquities. Egypt's rites, distant and poorly understood, came to seem merely mysterious.

The strangest turn came from medicine. An Arabic word for a bituminous substance, **mūmiyā**, ended up linked with Egyptian mummies in European markets. By the Middle Ages, powdered mummy, sold as [[mumia]], was treated as a genuine remedy that physicians and apothecaries prescribed for all sorts of ailments. For centuries, real mummies were therefore traded, then ground into medicine.

blocks.caption: An apothecary jar labeled "Mumia": powdered mummy sold as medicine.

blocks.text: In the Victorian era, painters used a pigment called "mummy brown," made from real ground-up mummies. When artists learned what it was made of, some reportedly buried their paint tubes in protest.
A body preserved for religious reasons had become a **commodity**, drifting ever further from the system that gave it meaning.

Egyptian tombs sometimes carry warnings meant to protect the burial from intruders. But an ancient belief in a supernatural curse that kills anyone who opens a tomb never existed. The **mummy's curse** is a modern invention, born of storytelling and a sensational press, not of Egyptian religion.

In **1922**, the British archaeologist [[Howard Carter]] discovered the tomb of [[Tutankhamun]]. That is the moment the myth took hold. [[Lord Carnarvon]], who financed the dig, died the following year after an illness. Newspapers linked his death to the tomb's supposed curse. Coincidence became legend.
The story sticks because half of it is real: a genuine tomb, a genuine mummy and a genuine death, folded into a supernatural narrative the evidence has never supported.

Film completed the transformation. In **1932**, *The Mummy*, starring [[Boris Karloff]], turned an archaeological object into a monster that moves, chases and takes revenge. Every mummy movie since borrows something from it. Bandages, a tomb and shuffling steps became shorthand the moment a story wants to say "danger from the past."

blocks.text: The real horror is not Egyptian religion, but what comes after: a body preserved to secure a place in the afterlife is stripped of that meaning and becomes the symbol of a past that refuses to stay buried. Beneath the wrappings, the mummy keeps a **human face**, and that is precisely why it unsettles. A corpse is supposed to disappear. A mummy does not, and that alone is enough, long after anyone believes in curses.
Made to protect a dead person, the mummy only became frightening once it was torn from its tomb: ground into medicine, turned into legend by the press, then brought to life by the movies.
